binders: p is an arbitrary sequence indexed by natural numbers, where p(n) is a real number equipped with a proof that 0≤p(n)≤1.
k is an arbitrary sequence of natural numbers indexed by natural numbers.
For each index n in the conclusion, G ranges over simple graphs with vertex set Fin n, and v ranges over vertices in Fin n.
hypotheses: For every natural number n, the exact real equality k(n)=10·(n-1)·p(n) holds, where k(n) and the truncated natural number n-1 are cast to Real and p(n) denotes the underlying real value.
As n tends to infinity through the natural numbers, the real sequence k(n)/log(n) converges to 0 in the usual real topology.
conclusions: For all sufficiently large natural numbers n, under the binomial random simple-graph law on n labeled vertices with edge probability p(n), the event that at least one vertex has degree exactly k(n) has real-valued measure at least 9/10.
mathematical_definitions: Fin n is the labeled vertex set {0,1,...,n-1}.
The graph law is the independent-edge binomial random graph on Fin n in which every unordered pair of distinct vertices is included as an edge with Bernoulli parameter p(n).
The degree of a vertex is the finite cardinality of its neighbor set.
The event at index n is {G : there exists v in Fin n such that degree_G(v)=k(n)}; the equality is exact natural-number equality.
Measure.real converts the extended-nonnegative measure of the event to a real number using toReal.
Eventually at the Nat atTop filter means that there is a natural bound N such that the asserted probability inequality holds for every n≥N.
Convergence to 0 at Nat atTop is ordinary convergence of the real sequence k(n)/log(n) as n grows without bound.
Natural subtraction is truncated before casting, so n-1 equals 0 at n=0; real division and Real.log are totalized at exceptional inputs.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every choice of edge-probability sequence p(n) in [0,1] and natural-number sequence k(n), if k(n) is exactly ten times (n-1)p(n) for every n and k(n) grows sublogarithmically in the sense that k(n)/log(n) tends to zero, then for all sufficiently large n an independent-edge random graph on n labeled vertices with edge probability p(n) has, with probability at least 9/10, some vertex whose degree is exactly k(n).

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The equation k(n)=10·(n-1)·p(n) is exact over the reals while k(n) is natural-valued, so it imposes an exact integrality compatibility condition on p(n) at every index.
Because p(n) lies in [0,1], the equation implies 0≤k(n)≤10(n-1), but it does not directly impose the graph-theoretic feasibility bound k(n)≤n-1.

The convergence hypothesis forces k(n)/log(n)→0 and hence eventually rules out persistent choices with k(n) comparable to n, but no separate positivity, divergence, monotonicity, or lower-growth condition on k is assumed.
At n=0 and n=1, the equation forces k(n)=0 because truncated n-1 is zero.
Real.log(0)=0 and Real.log(1)=0, while real division is totalized, so the first two quotient terms are defined rather than excluded; these finitely many terms do not affect convergence at infinity.
Fin 0 has no vertices, making the existential degree event empty at n=0, but the eventual conclusion may discard this and all other finitely many exceptional indices.
The implication is not inherently vacuous: for example, p(n)=0 and k(n)=0 satisfy both hypotheses, and for every positive n the resulting empty graph has vertices of degree zero with probability one.
The conclusion concerns the existence of at least one vertex of exact degree k(n), not degree at least k(n), not a fixed vertex, and not all vertices.

The probability value is Measure.real, hence an ENNReal-to-Real conversion; its intended interpretation as an ordinary probability relies on the graph law being finite and probability-normalized, as supplied by the binomial random-graph construction.
No assertion is made for every n, only for all sufficiently large n, and the threshold may depend on the entire sequences p and k.
The statement encodes independence and a common edge probability through binomialRandom, but it does not separately state those properties as hypotheses.
No rate of convergence for k(n)/log(n), no quantitative threshold for the eventual bound, and no uniformity over p or k are encoded.
ambiguities: The formal target unambiguously contains the factor 10 in k(n)=10·(n-1)·p(n); it does not indicate whether this factor is intended or a scaling mismatch relative to the ordinary expected degree (n-1)p(n).

The notation graphLaw.real is semantically the toReal conversion of a measure value; the proposition itself does not explicitly label the measure as a probability measure, although binomialRandom supplies that intended role.
The proposition does not explain why exact equality between an integer k(n) and the real expression 10·(n-1)·p(n) is the desired parameter relation.
No intended treatment of degenerate regimes such as p(n)=0, k(n)=0, or eventually empty graphs is stated beyond what follows from the formal definitions.
No source-level interpretation is available for the local package names; their supplied bodies determine the mathematical meaning used in this translation.
